Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 1–2:

﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ means the disbelievers of Quraysh, but the generality of the expression includes every disbeliever. Likewise, his saying after this, ﴿and those who believe﴾, means the Companions, but the generality of the expression is suitable for every believer. ﴿And hinder [others] from the way of Allah﴾: the verb ṣaddū may be understood as meaning "they turned away," in which case it is intransitive, or as meaning "they hindered the people," in which case it is transitive. The way of Allah is Islam and obedience. ﴿He has caused their deeds to go astray﴾, meaning He nullified and voided them. It was said that what is meant by their deeds here is what they spent at the Battle of Badr, since this verse was revealed after Badr, but the wording is more general than that. ﴿And believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾: this is a singling out and a special emphasis after the generality of his saying ﴿believe and do righteous deeds﴾. For this reason He reinforced it with the parenthetical clause, which is His saying ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾. ﴿And He has rectified their condition﴾: it was said that the meaning is that He set right their state and affairs. The literal meaning of al-bāl is the thought that is in the heart, and when the heart is sound, the whole body is sound. So the meaning is the rectification of their religion through faith, sincerity, and piety.

ـ﴿فَضَرْبَ ٱلرِّقَابِ﴾ (Fa-darba al-riqab, "so strike the necks"): the original form is "fa-idribu al-riqab darban," then the verb was deleted and the verbal noun (masdar) was put in its place. The intended meaning is "kill them." It was expressed as "striking the necks" because that is the most common manner of killing.

﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَآ أَثْخَنتُمُوهُمْ﴾ (Until when you have subdued them): i.e., you have defeated them. Ith-khan (overwhelming) means that killing and taking captives become abundant among them.

﴿فَشُدُّواْ ٱلْوَثَاقَ﴾ (then bind the bonds): an expression for taking captives.

﴿فَإِمَّا مَنًّا بَعْدُ وَإِمَّا فِدَآءً﴾ (Then either grace afterward or ransom): al-mann (grace) is manumission, and al-fida' (ransom) is freeing the captive in exchange for property. Both are permissible. The school of Malik holds that the imam has a choice regarding captives among five things: grace, ransom, killing, enslavement, and imposing the jizya (poll tax). It has been said that neither grace nor ransom is permitted, because the verse was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿فَٱقْتُلُواْ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (Then kill the polytheists) [al-Tawba: 5], so according to this view only killing them is permitted. The correct view is that the verse is muhkam (not abrogated), and mannan and fida' are in the accusative as verbal nouns (masdar), with two implied verbs governing them.

﴿حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا﴾ (Until war lays down its burdens): al-awzar in the language means the loads, so the meaning is "until its loads depart and cease," and these are its implements (ālāt). It has been said that al-awzar means sins, because war necessarily involves sin on one of the two sides. The end intended here is disputed. It has been said: until they all submit, and then war lays down its burdens. It has been said: until you kill them and overpower them. It has been said: until Jesus son of Mary descends. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the apparent sense of the wording is a metaphor meaning the commitment to the matter perpetually, as when you say, "I will do that until the Day of Resurrection."

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (That): its estimated sense is "the matter is that."

﴿وَلَوْ يَشَآءُ اللَّهُ لاَنْتَصَرَ مِنْهُمْ﴾ (And had God willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them): or, had God willed, He would have destroyed the disbelievers with a punishment from Himself, but He, exalted is He, willed to test the believers and to make some of the people a trial for others.

﴿ʿArrafahā lahum﴾ means: He made them know their dwellings therein; so it is from ma'rifah (knowledge). It was also said: its meaning is that He made it fragrant for them, so it is from al-'arf, which is pleasant scent. And it was said: its meaning is that He honoured it and raised it up, so it is from al-a'raf, which are the mountains.

﴿Fa-ta'san lahum﴾ means stumbling and destruction. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its governing verb is an implied verb; on this verb is coordinated "and He has caused their deeds to go astray" (wa-aḍalla a'mālahum).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 10:

﴿And for the disbelievers is the like thereof﴾ That is, for the disbelievers of Quraysh are the like of the end of the earlier disbelievers: destruction and annihilation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 11:

﴿Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe﴾, that is, their Guardian (waliyy) and Helper (nasir). Likewise, ﴿and the disbelievers have no protector (mawla)﴾ means: they have no helper. It is not valid for mawla to mean "master" (sayyid) here, because Allah is the mawla of both believers and disbelievers in this sense. There is no contradiction between this verse and His words: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Mawla﴾ [al-An'am: 62], because the meaning of mawla differs in the two places. The meaning of ﴿their true Mawla﴾ is: their Lord (rabb). This applies generally to all creation, unlike ﴿Allah is the Mawla of those who believe﴾, which is specific to the believers, since it carries the meaning of wali (guardian) and nasir (helper).

Their eating like cattle eat: a description of how much they eat, and of their heedlessness in reflection, like beasts.

Note on the source text: the Qur'anic quotation is ﴿وَيَأْكُلُونَ كَمَا تَأْكُلُ ٱلأَنْعَامُ﴾, rendered in the translation above. The Qur'anic verse reads: ﴿And they eat as cattle eat﴾.

"from your town which has expelled you": that is, Makkah. His (ﷺ) departure (khurūj) was at the time of the Hijrah, and the expulsion is attributed to the town, while what is meant is its people, because they harmed him until he left. "We destroyed them": the pronoun refers to the earlier towns mentioned in His saying: ﴿And how many a town﴾, and it is in the plural by considering the meaning; what is meant by "We destroyed them" is: its people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verses 14–15:

﴿Is he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾ means: upon a proof (ḥujja). By this is meant the Prophet (ﷺ), just as by his saying ﴿like one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him﴾ is meant the Quraysh. The wording, however, is more general than that.

﴿The likeness of Paradise﴾ has been mentioned in Surah al-Ra'd [13:35]. ﴿Unchanging (ghayr āsin)﴾ means: not altering. ﴿Is he like one who abides forever in the Fire?﴾ Its implied sense (taqdīr) is: Is the likeness of the people of the Paradise described (as above) like one who abides forever in the Fire? This is omitted by way of the implied sense, and the intended meaning is negation. It was omitted because the earlier implied sense indicates it, namely his saying: ﴿Is he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾.

**﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾**: he means the hypocrites. The verb "yastami'un" (they listen) is given in the plural to honor the meaning of "man" (among them).

**﴿They say to those who were given knowledge﴾**: it is narrated that this refers to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him). **﴿"What did he just say?"﴾** They used to say this in one of two ways: either out of contempt for his speech, as if they were saying, "What benefit is there in it?", or out of ignorance and forgetfulness, since they were turned away from it at the time he was speaking. "Anfan" means "just now," the recently passed hour, and its root is from "isti'naftu al-shay'" (I began the thing), meaning I started it anew.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 17:

﴿And those who were guided – He increases them in guidance﴾. He means the believers. The pronoun in "increases them" refers either to God Most High or to the speech about which the hypocrites said: "What did he say just now?" It has also been said: by "those who were guided" he means a group of Christians who believed in our master Muhammad (ﷺ); their being guided is their faith in Jesus, and the increase in their guidance is their Islam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 18:

﴿Do they await anything but the Hour?﴾ The pronoun (*damir*) refers to the hypocrites. The meaning is: do they await anything but the Hour, because it is near? ﴿Its signs have already come﴾, that is, its indications (*ʿalamat*). Among what has already come of them is the mission of our master Muhammad (ﷺ), for he said: "I am one of the signs of the Hour, and I and the Hour have been sent like these two," [referring to his two fingers].

﴿How, then, for them will be their reminder when it comes to them?﴾ That is: how will they have any reminder when the Hour comes upon them suddenly? Then they will be unable to act, and repentance will not benefit them. The agent (*fa'il*) of "came to them" is "the Hour," and "their reminder" is the subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is the interrogative mentioned above, and what is meant by it is denial of such a possibility (*istib'ad*).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 19:

﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾. That is, persist in knowledge of this. Some scholars used this verse as evidence that reflection and knowledge come before action, because He placed His saying "so know" before His saying "and seek forgiveness". ﴿And Allah knows your movement [about] and your resting place﴾. It was said: "your movement" refers to your activity in this world, and "your resting place" to your residence in the graves. It was also said: "your movement" refers to your activity while awake, and "your resting place" to your sleep.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verses 20–21:

﴿Why has a surah not been sent down?﴾ The believers would say this out of eagerness for the descent of the Qur'an and desire for it, for they rejoiced in it and felt distress at its delay. ﴿Clear (muḥkamah)﴾ may mean that it contains no abrogated ruling (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one), or it may mean perfected (mutqanah). Ibn Mas'ud read "سورة محدثة" (sūratun muḥdathah), meaning "a newly revealed surah." ﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease looking at you﴾ refers to the hypocrites. Their looking was that of one in intense fear of being killed, because the gaze of the frightened is close to the gaze of one who has fainted. ﴿So woe to them (fa-awlā lahum)﴾ has two interpretations regarding its meaning. The first is that "أولى" (awlā) means "more deserving," and its predicate in this case is "طاعة" (ṭāʿah, obedience). The meaning is that obedience and good speech are more fitting and more deserving for them. The second is that "أولى لهم" is an expression meaning threat and invocation against them, like your saying "ويل لهم" (woe to them). From this, "أولى لك فأولى" is also derived. On this view, one stops at "أولى لهم," and "طاعة" begins a new sentence, with the implied meaning: "obedience and good speech are more fitting," or "what is required of them is obedience and good speech." Their saying to you, O Muhammad, "obedience and good speech" was with their tongues, not their hearts. ﴿And when the matter is resolved (fa-idhā ʿazama al-amr)﴾: the resolve is ascribed to the matter figuratively (majāzan, meaning a figurative usage), as in your saying "نهاره صائم وليله قائم" (his day is fasting and his night is standing in prayer). ﴿They would have been true to God (ṣadaqū Allāh)﴾ may mean truthfulness of the tongue, or truthfulness of resolve and intention, and the latter is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 22:

﴿So is it to be expected of you, if you were to take charge, that you would cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ This is an address to the hypocrites mentioned earlier. The discourse shifts from the third person (absence) to the second person (direct address), to make the rebuke more forceful. The meaning is: Is anything to be expected from you, if you take charge, other than corruption on the earth and the severing of kinship? The meaning of "tawallaytum" (توليتم, you took charge) is: you became rulers over the people and the matter came into your hands. On this basis it has been said that the verse was revealed concerning the Banu Umayya. And it has been said: its meaning is that you turned away from Islam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 47, verses 25–27:

﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾ was revealed concerning the hypocrites who became hypocrites after their Islam. It is also said that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who had recognized the prophethood of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) from the Torah and then disbelieved in him. ﴿Satan made it seem fair to them﴾, meaning he adorned it for them and deluded them and gave them false hopes, ﴿and granted them long hopes﴾, meaning he extended for them false wishes and expectations. The agent is Satan, though it is also said to be God, may He be exalted, but the first view is more apparent, because of the consistency of the pronoun between the two agents in ﴿sawwala﴾ (made fair) and ﴿amla﴾ (granted respite). ﴿"We will obey you in part of the matter"﴾: the Jews said this to the hypocrites, and by "part of the matter" they meant opposing the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and fighting him. ﴿So how will it be when the angels take them in death?﴾ meaning, how will their condition be when the angels take their souls? This refers to the Angel of Death and those with him. The fa' (فَ, "so") is a connective linking the speech with what came before it. The meaning is: this is their dismay at the mention of fighting, so how will their condition be at the time of death? ﴿striking their faces﴾: the subject of the verb is the angels. It is also said that it refers to the disbelievers, meaning they strike their own faces, but this view is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verses 29–32:

﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a sickness think that Allah will never bring out their malice?﴾ Its meaning: the hypocrites thought that Allah would never expose them. Al-ghadb (rancor) means spite, and what is meant here is hypocrisy and hatred toward Islam and its people. ﴿And if We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have known them by their marks.﴾ That is, if We willed, We would have shown you the hypocrites by their very persons, so that you would recognize them by their signs. But Allah concealed them, out of mercy toward them and toward their relatives among the Muslims. It is narrated that Allah did not mention any one of them by name. ﴿And you will surely know them by the tone of their speech.﴾ The meaning of lahn al-qawl (the tone of speech) is its intent and manner. It is said: lahn is that whose meaning is hidden, like allusion and indirect insinuation. The meaning is that the Prophet (ﷺ) would recognize them from the indications of their speech, even though Allah did not identify them to him individually. ﴿And We will surely test you﴾ That is, We will examine you. ﴿Until We know﴾ That is, We will know it with an outward knowledge existing in reality, by which the proof is established against you. Allah knew things before their occurrence, but He willed to establish the proof upon His servants by what proceeds from them. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad, when he recited this verse, would weep and say: "O Allah, do not test us, for when You test us You expose us and tear away our veils." ﴿And they opposed the Messenger﴾ That is, they contradicted him and were hostile to him. The verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and it is said: concerning the Jews.

The meaning is that the Prophet (ﷺ) would recognize them from the indications of their speech, even though Allah did not identify them to him individually. ﴿And We will surely test you﴾ That is, We will examine you. ﴿Until We know﴾ That is, We will know it with an outward knowledge existing in reality, by which the proof is established against you. Allah knew things before their occurrence, but He willed to establish the proof upon His servants by what proceeds from them. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad, when he recited this verse, would weep and say: "O Allah, do not test us, for when You test us You expose us and tear away our veils." ﴿And they opposed the Messenger﴾ That is, they contradicted him and were hostile to him. The verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and it is said: concerning the Jews.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 33:

﴿And do not render your deeds void﴾ may bear four meanings. The first: do not render your deeds void by disbelief after belief. The second: do not render your good deeds void by committing evil deeds; this is mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, and it follows the school of the Mu'tazilah, in contrast to the Ash'ariyyah, whose position is that evil deeds do not void good deeds. The third: do not render your deeds void through showing off (riya') and self-admiration ('ujb). The fourth: do not render your deeds void by cutting them off before they are completed. The jurists have taken the verse in this sense, and by it they argue that whoever begins a voluntary act of worship (nafilah) may not discontinue it. This is the most remote of these meanings. The first is the most apparent, given His words before it concerning the disbelievers or hypocrites: ﴿and He will render their deeds void﴾. So it is as if He says: O you who believe, do not render your deeds void as these people did, whose deeds Allah rendered void by their disbelief, their turning others away from the way of Allah, and their opposition to the Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 34:

﴿So Allah will never forgive them﴾. This is a definite statement that whoever dies in disbelief, Allah will not forgive him, and the Muslims have reached consensus (ijma') on this.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 35:

﴿So do not weaken and call to peace﴾ meaning: do not be feeble in fighting the disbelievers, and do not initiate reconciliation with them. It is like His saying: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61]. ﴿And He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾ meaning: He will not diminish for you the rewards of your deeds. It is said: "wataru al-rajul ata'ruhu" (وترت الرجال أتره) when one diminishes something of him, or takes away his property.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 36–37:

﴿And He does not ask you for your wealth.﴾ That is, He does not ask all of it from you; He only asks of you what is light for you, such as a quarter of a tenth (rub' al-'ushr), and that is light. ﴿If He were to ask it of you and press you (yuhfikum), you would be stingy (tabkhalu).﴾ The meaning of yuhfikum is that He insists upon you (yulihhu 'alaykum), and al-ihfa' (pressing) is the most severe form of asking. Tabkhalu is the answer of the conditional clause. ﴿And He would bring forth your malice (adghanakum).﴾ The agent is God Most High, or stinginess (al-bukhl), and the meaning is that He brings forth what is in your hearts of stinginess and aversion to spending.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 47, verse 38:

﴿These﴾ is in the accusative case as a specification (ʿalā al-takhṣīṣ), or it is a vocative (munādā). ﴿You are called to spend in the way of Allah﴾, meaning jihad and zakat. ﴿And whoever is stingy, he is only stingy against himself﴾, i.e., the harm of his stinginess falls only upon himself, as if he has withheld from himself the reward that he deserves by spending. ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾, i.e., He will bring a people of a different character than you, rather eager to spend in the way of Allah. It has been said that this address is to the Quraysh, and "another people" refers to the Ansar; but this is weak, because the surah is Madani and the Ansar were present. It has also been said that the address is to everyone who was in Medina at that time, and "the people" are the people of Yemen, and it has been said they are the Persians.
